chapter_theme: Short speeches of the five lands: women waiting through the rains and the seasons for men gone to the waste (281-283, 285, 287, 289, 290), men remembering and reassuring the hill-girl (286, 291, 300), the friend's curses, counsel and pleas in secret love (284, 292, 294, 297, 298), and the wife's grief at the husband's other women (293, 295, 296), with two poems weighing love against heaven and the world (288, 300).

281.reading: The woman asks her bright-jewelled friend whether their man has gone into the forest where hills crowd together, his curly head bright with the white leaf from the crown of the palmyra that grows thick on white sand and with the pale flowers of the neem.
281.nuance: She sees him in his going-out dress, palmyra leaf and neem flowers on his head, the kind of adornment worn by men setting out as warriors; the whole poem is one picture and one question, and the question (கொல்லோ) lets her hold off knowing. உளைத்தலை could also be the tufted head of a horse.

thinai_evidence.note: she asks whether he has already left on the hill-forest road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative சேயிழை names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

282.reading: The friend asks whether their man, seeing the cool clearing turning toward the rains, where the young fawn of the deer nibbles the dark leaf of the seedling sprung on the red ground of ripe millet, will not say that her bangles must be slipping off like the new hollow flowers of white koothalam dropping from their stems on the water-bright slope.
282.nuance: The friend hopes the season itself will speak for the woman: the land he crosses shows him the rains, and she wants him to read her slipping bangles there. Line 7 (ஆர்கழல் புகுவ) is hard to construe; the falling-flower sense is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the field facing the rains is the season he should come back by

comparisons.tenor: her bangles slipping off her wasted arms

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: நமர் suggests the friend speaks to the woman; the colophon gives only the speaker

283.reading: The woman tells her friend that he left after showing her plainly the force of what he had said, that those who waste what they have are not counted as men and that the life of the poor is more shameful even than begging, and went by the waterless road through the long old waste where a hawk watches the reeking flesh of travellers killed by bandits whose spears kill like Death.
283.nuance: She quotes his reasons almost as maxims and then sets them against the road: the argument that sent him is clear (தெளியக் காட்டி), and what waits on the road is a hawk over the bodies of men robbed of what they carried. The poem does not say whether she accepts the argument.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone for wealth across the waterless waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative வாழி தோழி names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

284.reading: The friend says that, whether the man of the land where many bright red kaanthal open together on the boulder of the village common like the spotted face of a fighting elephant proves good or not, the people of this small village, living wretchedly in their huts below the white waterfall that drops from the hill, will blame us, or care nothing for us.
284.nuance: Line 5 (நம்மே சுவரோ தம்மிலர் கொல்லோ) is hard to divide, and the reading 'will they blame us' is a guess; what is clear is the friend weighing the lover's worth against the village's judgment, and finding the village careless either way.

thinai_evidence.note: kaanthal on the rock and the hill waterfall

comparisons.tenor: the red kaanthal massed on the rock

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the man is spoken of in the third person (நாடன்); the colophon gives only the speaker

285.reading: The woman asks her friend where he can be, who crossed the sky-high mountains where a lone hawk sits on the top of the nyemai tree craving flesh: day after day passes and he does not come, every limit of time passes and he does not appear, though this is the season he named; is the bird calling again and again to its dull-backed mate for delight nothing to his eyes?
285.nuance: The repeated words of lines 1 and 2 (வைகல் வைகல் வைகவும், எல்லா எல்லை எல்லையும்) make the days pile up in the sound. Lines 5 and 6 are hard; the bird and its mate are read as the season's sign the man ignores. The lone hawk waiting for flesh is a mood of the road, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits for one who crossed the mountains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

iraicchi.act: the male bird calls to its mate again and again so that they may delight together
iraicchi.sense: at this season even birds call their mates, yet he does not come to her

286.reading: The man says he seems to see, as he thinks of it, the look of the hill-girl with wide rain-cool eyes, full of pride and soft smiling, her mouth red and lovely where nectar wells by her sharp teeth, her hair dark like rippled sand and fragrant with agil and sandal.
286.nuance: The whole poem is one noun phrase hanging on நோக்கே, the last word: after the mouth, the hair and the eyes, what memory finally holds is a look, proud and smiling at once.

thinai_evidence.note: the beloved is a girl of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he speaks to himself; the colophon gives only the speaker

287.reading: The speaker asks her friend whether their lover will forsake them even after seeing it: the time when the great roaring cloud, having drunk the sea, cannot climb the sky and holds itself back, gathering toward the many rich hills, like women heavy with a first child who, at the end of their months, cannot move and crave green tamarind.
287.nuance: The cloud is pregnant with rain as women are with child, and the season it brings is the one he promised; the simile makes the rain season itself a time of fulfilment he would be failing.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain clouds gather: the season of return

comparisons.tenor: the rain clouds slow and heavy with water

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names the friend as speaker, but the poem addresses தோழி and speaks of காதலர், which reads as the woman's voice; see source_issues

288.reading: The woman says that because the lord of the great hill country, where monkeys sit together eating tender shoots on the slope where pepper grows, is dear to her, even the hurt that comes from kin is sweeter than the world of the gods that is called sweet.
288.nuance: Whose kin (இனத்தின்) cause the hurt is not said: her own family's anger at the affair, or his people's coldness. The monkeys that sit together (ஒருங்கு) eating may hint at a troop that keeps its members, but the poem does not draw this, so they stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: pepper slopes and monkeys of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; the colophon gives only the speaker

289.reading: The woman tells her friend that, growing day by day like the waxing moon, the grief that loosened the bangles on her wrist has left her shrunk like a crushed sprout; besides the pain of his not being near, the rain has set in thick, and this clamouring town pities her more than she pities him out in the rain.
289.nuance: The town here is not the hostile gossip of other poems but a chorus of pity, and its pity measures her own: she grieves for him in the rain, the town grieves for her. Line 6 (பட்ட மாரி படாஅக் கண்ணும்) is hard and the reading of it is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come while he is away

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

290.reading: The woman asks whether those who tell her to bear her love do not know what it is, or are themselves that strong: if she does not see her lover, with a heart where clinging grief has swelled, she will waste away little by little like the small foam that breaks on a rock in deep water.
290.nuance: The image gives no crash, only foam dissolving where it strikes; the doubled மெல்ல மெல்ல makes the dissolution slow. The poet is named from this simile (கல்பொரு சிறுநுரையார்).

thinai_evidence.note: lament of one who will fade without him

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she answers those who counsel endurance; the colophon gives only the speaker

291.reading: The man says that the clapper in the hand of the hill-girl driving parrots from the millet on the burnt clearing makes a call sweeter than music, so the parrots take it for one of their own and will not rise; and her eyes, which wept in vexation at that, were like the many-petalled kuvalai of the deep hill pool, ruffled by bees and taking the cool drops.
291.nuance: The joke turns on her sweetness: she fails at her work because her voice is too lovely, and her vexed tears only add a second beauty. The man watches both.

thinai_evidence.note: a hill girl guarding millet from parrots

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; the colophon gives only the speaker

292.reading: The friend curses her mother: as Nannan, when a bright-browed girl who had gone to bathe ate a green fruit the stream carried down, refused eighty-one elephants and a golden doll of her weight in amends and chose to kill a woman, so may her mother go to endless hell, who, since a smiling guest came one day, has not slept, as in a town that faces enemies.
292.nuance: The curse is wildly out of proportion, and that is the point: one visit from a smiling guest has turned the house into a town under siege, and the friend answers with the worst story of cruelty she knows, a chief who would take no ransom for a girl's small fault.

thinai_evidence.note: the mother's watch keeps the lovers apart

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the speaker curses the mother in the third person, perhaps with the man in hearing; the colophon gives only the speaker

293.reading: The wife says she is to be pitied: the bright-jewelled one, lovely as the old town of Aathi Aruman where people go home with palmyra kernels from tall dark palms whose spathes give small fibrous fruit, comes there, her leaf-skirt of white lilies beating in turn on her spotted thighs, to see the husband.
293.nuance: The rival is praised before she is resented: the wife grants her the beauty of a famous chief's old town and then ends on herself, அளியேன் யானே. Line 1 (கள்ளிற் கேளிர் ஆத்திரை) is obscure: ஆத்திரை may be a place or a person, and the poet's name is taken from it.

thinai_evidence.note: another woman comes for the husband

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; the colophon gives only the speaker

294.reading: The friend says that after sea-bathing, resting in the shore grove and dancing in the garlanded troop, he came suddenly like a stranger, embraced her and went, and gossip spread; yet he never left her side, and himself gave the green-leaf skirt that swings on her spotted hips with its fresh shoots; now mother keeps her guarded.
294.nuance: The gift of a leaf-skirt is a lover's pledge, and the friend sets it against his stranger-like coming and going: the bond is real, and now the mother's watch makes marriage the only road. The last line (காத்தோம் பல்லே) is hard to divide.

thinai_evidence.note: sea-bathing and the shore grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the man is spoken of in the third person; the colophon gives only the speaker

295.reading: The friend tells the man that he comes with the festival in a crowd of women bright with leaves worn as skirts, strung, put on and tucked in the hair, and that this town says the festival has truly begun now that the lovely young girl of a poor house that lives on a single cow has come.
295.nuance: The town's praise of the new girl is reported by the friend as an accusation: 'the festival has come' now means 'your new woman has come', and the poverty of her house (one cow) sharpens the sting.

thinai_evidence.note: the man comes to the festival with other women

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend addresses the man (நீயே); the colophon gives only the speaker

296.reading: The woman tells her friend not to stand before the lord of the cool shore, where the stork sitting on the swaying punnai bough, tired of the small fish of the creek, longs for the toddy-scented neythal among the paddy of the field, and rebuke him harshly, as she had resolved, asking whether it suits him to forsake one who is in such a state.
296.nuance: She forbids the rebuke while repeating it in full, so the reproach is spoken after all, through the friend's resolve. The stork leaving the creek's fish for the field is the hidden picture of his straying.

thinai_evidence.note: the stork on the punnai of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses a stork of her own shore, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

297.reading: The friend says she understood surely, before he did, that the right course was for the two to go off together, speaking good words of the wide rocky waste where the cairns heaped with leaves over travellers who stood against the bow-bearing bandits and died look like a village.
297.nuance: The friend takes credit for the elopement plan, and lays its road out in its worst colours, a village of graves; the danger is not hidden from the girl but made part of the choice.

thinai_evidence.note: elopement through the waste land

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the man is spoken of in the third person; the colophon gives only the speaker

298.reading: The friend asks the woman to think of the sorrowful look of the man who comes slowly again and again to their street, rarely opens his mouth to say sweet words and stays each day with his colour changed: his long standing at the back aims at something else, like the young she-elephants that Akuthai's father, of sweet strong toddy, gave as gifts to the singing women with small white-tipped sticks.
298.nuance: The simile is the hard part: what the gift and the waiting share seems to be that each is an outward act aimed at something beyond itself, the chief's gift at the singers' praise, the man's patience at the girl. The friend thus casts the lover as a suppliant whose silence is a request.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover waiting for the girl's consent

comparisons.tenor: his long waiting at the back

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி marks the friend speaking to the woman; the colophon gives only the speaker

299.reading: The woman asks her friend what this is: in the shade of the clustered punnai on the dune of the shore grove where the old sea's waves play and birds cry, on the day their tryst came true, her eyes saw the lord of the shore and her ears heard his words; and now her wide soft shoulders take on great beauty when he joins her and waste when he leaves.
299.nuance: Eyes and ears are named as the witnesses that did the harm, each with மன் (once, and no more); the body that now swells and wastes with his coming and going is the only record left.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea and the shore grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

300.reading: The man tells the dark girl with fine spots like the pollen of the deep-water lotus, with heaped dark hair smelling of kuvalai and a honeyed red mouth smelling of aambal, that she fears his very word 'do not fear'; but he would not think of leaving her friendship even if he gained the sea-ringed world where the short-legged swan rests on heaped sand.
300.nuance: The setting of நீயே against யானே divides the poem between her fear and his oath. The swan resting on heaped sand is a shore image of rest, put inside the very world he says he would refuse.

thinai_evidence.note: reassurance after union in secret love

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man addresses the girl (மாஅயோயே); the colophon gives only the speaker

links.note: Kuruntokai 283 reports the man's maxim that the life of those who have nothing is more shameful even than begging, and he leaves for wealth; Kural 1064 says the worth that will not beg even when nothing is left is too great for the world to hold. On the reading that 283 ranks poverty below begging, the two rank the same states in opposite order.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the destitute man who refuses to beg the height of dignity, while the akam hero's maxim makes destitution itself the deepest shame, so the poems show that the urge to go for wealth rested on a ranking of poverty and begging the Kural explicitly reverses.

links.note: Kural 1103: the man asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world is sweeter than sleep on the beloved's soft arms; Kuruntokai 288: the woman asks whether the world of the gods is sweeter even than the hurt that comes from kin because of her lover.
links.teaches: The couplet weighs heaven against the joy of love, the poem weighs it against love's pain, so the woman's claim is the stronger: not only the embrace but even the suffering it brings outweighs the gods' world.

links.note: Kural 1233: the shoulders that swelled on the day of union now seem to announce the parting; Kuruntokai 299: the woman's shoulders gain beauty when he joins her and waste when he leaves, after the tryst on the shore.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the swelling and the wasting as public evidence that others read, while the poem gives them as the woman's own bewildered discovery, tied to the day her eyes saw him and her ears heard him, so the same bodily sign is both the town's proof and her private record.

links.note: Kural 1130: he lives joyfully in her heart, while the town says he is unloving and lives apart; Kuruntokai 289: she grieves for him out in the rain, and the clamouring town grieves for her more.
links.teaches: In both the woman's thought goes out to the absent man while the town's goes to her plight, but the town's verdict differs, blame in the Kural and pity in the poem, so the town's talk in akam is not fixed as hostile gossip and can be her chorus.

links.note: Akananuru 45, told to bear up, the woman answers with the dangers of his road, the gossip and her own coming madness like Aathi Manthi's; Kuruntokai 290 answers the same counsel ('bear your love') by saying she will waste away like foam on a rock.
links.teaches: The two poems answer the same counsel to endure in opposite registers, one with public ruin and a famous madness, the other with a silent dissolving, which shows that the heroine's refusal of endurance could be voiced as loud breakdown or as quiet vanishing.

links.note: Kuruntokai 73 (Paranar) tells of the Kosar who cut down Nannan's fragrant mango and drove him from his land; Kuruntokai 292 (Paranar) tells of Nannan killing a girl who ate a green fruit the stream carried down, refusing eighty-one elephants and her weight in gold.
links.teaches: Read together, Paranar's two poems hold both halves of one tale, the cruelty over a fruit and the tree's later felling, and each friend uses a different half: one as a model of hard scheming, the other as the type of cruelty to curse a watchful mother with.

links.note: Purananuru 233 names Akuthai as the strong one whose elephants never ran short for those who came for gifts; Kuruntokai 298 recalls the young she-elephants Akuthai's father gave to singing women and likens the lover's long waiting to that gift.
links.teaches: The puram lament knows the house of Akuthai only as givers of elephants, and the akam friend turns that known generosity into a figure for a lover's patience, so a patron's fame for gifts served akam as a ready image of an act that waits on a return.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 300 the man says he would not leave her even for the sea-ringed world; in Kuruntokai 288 the woman says even the hurt love brings is sweeter than the world of the gods.
links.teaches: The man measures his love against earthly rule and the woman against heaven, so the two speakers of kalavu each renounce the highest good of their own sphere, kingship for him, the gods' world for her.

source_issues: Kuruntokai colophons give only the speaker (… கூற்று), so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem; each item says so in its note.
kuruntokai:283 line 3 (தெளிய) was repaired from a TSCII leftover (தௌிய); the repair reads correctly.
kuruntokai:293 line 8 is the tamilvu.org reading that replaced ours (flag); marked as printed.
kuruntokai:287: the colophon says தோழி கூற்று, but the poem addresses தோழி and speaks of காதலர், which reads as the woman's voice; the colophon is kept and the doubt recorded here.
Thinai differs from the colophon in 282 (mullai: the field facing the rains, against பாலை) and 297 (paalai: the elopement through the waste, against குறிஞ்சி).
Hard lines, marked uncertain: 282 line 7 (ஆர்கழல் புகுவ), 284 line 5 (நம்மே சுவரோ தம்மிலர்), 285 lines 5-6, 289 line 6, 293 line 1 (ஆத்திரை), 294 line 8 (காத்தோம் பல்லே), 298 lines 5-8 (the simile).
